  draw a personal conclusion that the document does not state itself.

content:
1	The first recorded description of the social interactions that could be enabled
     2	through networking was a series of memos written by J.C.R. Licklider of MIT in
     3	August 1962 discussing his “Galactic Network” concept. He envisioned a globally
     4	interconnected set of computers through which everyone could quickly access
     5	data and programs from any site. In spirit, the concept was very much like the
     6	Internet of today. Licklider was the first head of the computer research program
     7	at DARPA,4
     8	 starting in October 1962. While at DARPA he convinced his successors
     9	at DARPA, Ivan Sutherland, Bob Taylor, and MIT researcher Lawrence G. Roberts,
    10	of the importance of this networking concept.
    11	Leonard Kleinrock at MIT published the first paper on packet switching theory in
    12	July 1961 and the first book on the subject in 1964. Kleinrock convinced Roberts
    13	of the theoretical feasibility of communications using packets rather than
    14	circuits, which was a major step along the path towards computer networking.
    15	The other key step was to make the computers talk together. To explore this,
    16	in 1965 working with Thomas Merrill, Roberts connected the TX-2 computer in
    17	Mass. to the Q-32 in California with a low speed dial-up telephone line creating
    18	the first (however small) wide-area computer network ever built. The result
    19	of this experiment was the realization that the time-shared computers could
    20	work well together, running programs and retrieving data as necessary on the
    21	remote machine, but that the circuit switched telephone system was totally
    22	inadequate for the job. Kleinrock’s conviction of the need for packet switching
    23	was confirmed.
    24	In late 1966 Roberts went to DARPA to develop the computer network concept
    25	and quickly put together his plan for the “ARPANET”, publishing it in 1967. At the
    26	conference where he presented the paper, there was also a paper on a packet
    27	network concept from the UK by Donald Davies and Roger Scantlebury of NPL.
    28	Scantlebury told Roberts about the NPL work as well as that of Paul Baran and
    29	others at RAND. The RAND group had written a paper on packet switching
    30	networks for secure voice in the military in 1964. It happened that the work at
    31	MIT (1961-1967), at RAND (1962-1965), and at NPL (1964-1967) had all proceeded in
    32	parallel without any of the researchers knowing about the other work. The word
    33	“packet” was adopted from the work at NPL and the proposed line speed to be
    34	used in the ARPANET design was upgraded from 2.4 kbps to 50 kbps.5
    35	In August 1968, after Roberts and the DARPA funded community had refined the
    36	overall structure and specifications for the ARPANET, an RFQ was released by
    37	DARPA for the development of one of the key components, the packet switches
    38	called Interface Message Processors (IMP’s).
    39	The RFQ was won in December 1968 by a group headed by Frank Heart at Bolt
    40	Beranek and Newman (BBN). As the BBN team worked on the IMP’s with Bob
    41	Kahn playing a major role in the overall ARPANET architectural design, the
    42	network topology and economics were designed and optimized by Roberts working with Howard Frank and
    43	his team at Network Analysis Corporation, and the network
    44	measurement system was prepared by Kleinrock’s team at UCLA.6
    45	Due to Kleinrock’s early development of packet switching theory and his focus on analysis, design
    46	and measurement, his Network Measurement Center at UCLA was selected to be the first node on
    47	the ARPANET. All this came together in September 1969 when BBN installed the first IMP at UCLA
    48	and the first host computer was connected. Doug Engelbart’s project on “Augmentation of Human
    49	Intellect” (which included NLS, an early hypertext system) at Stanford Research Institute (SRI)
    50	provided a second node. SRI supported the Network Information Center, led by Elizabeth (Jake)
    51	Feinler and including functions such as maintaining tables of host name to address mapping as well
    52	as a directory of the RFC’s.
    53	One month later, when SRI was connected to the ARPANET, the first host-to-host message was sent
    54	from Kleinrock’s laboratory to SRI. Two more nodes were added at UC Santa Barbara and University
    55	of Utah. These last two nodes incorporated application visualization projects, with Glen Culler and
    56	Burton Fried at UCSB investigating methods for display of mathematical functions using storage
    57	displays to deal with the problem of refresh over the net, and Robert Taylor and Ivan Sutherland at
    58	Utah investigating methods of 3-D representations over the net. Thus, by the end of 1969, four host
    59	computers were connected together into the initial ARPANET, and the budding Internet was off the
    60	ground. Even at this early stage, it should be noted that the networking research incorporated both
    61	work on the underlying network and work on how to utilize the network. This tradition continues to
    62	this day.
    63	Computers were added quickly to the ARPANET during the following years, and work proceeded on
    64	completing a functionally complete Host-to-Host protocol and other network software. In December
    65	1970 the Network Working Group (NWG) working under S. Crocker finished the initial ARPANET
    66	Host-to-Host protocol, called the Network Control Protocol (NCP). As the ARPANET sites completed
    67	implementing NCP during the period 1971-1972, the network users finally could begin to develop
    68	applications.
    69	In October 1972, Kahn organized a large, very successful demonstration of the ARPANET at the
    70	International Computer Communication Conference (ICCC). This was the first public demonstration
    71	of this new network technology to the public. It was also in 1972 that the initial “hot”
    72	application,
    73	electronic mail, was introduced. In March Ray Tomlinson at BBN wrote the basic email message send
    74	and read software, motivated by the need of the ARPANET developers for an easy coordination
    75	mechanism. In July, Roberts expanded its utility by writing the first email utility program to list,
    76	selectively read, file, forward, and respond to messages. From there email took off as the largest
    77	network application for over a decade. This was a harbinger of the kind of activity we see on the
    78	World Wide Web today, namely, the enormous growth of all kinds of “people-to-people” traffic.

- Roberts was an MIT researcher whom J.C.R. Licklider, the first head of the computer research program at DARPA, "convinced ... of the importance of this networking concept" (doc.txt).
- He was persuaded by Kleinrock that packet-based communication was viable: "Kleinrock convinced Roberts of the theoretical feasibility of communications using packets rather than circuits, which was a major step along the path towards computer networking" (doc.txt).
- In 1965, Roberts built the first wide-area computer network: "in 1965 working with Thomas Merrill, Roberts connected the TX-2 computer in Mass. to the Q-32 in California with a low speed dial-up telephone line creating the first (however small) wide-area computer network ever built" (doc.txt). The experiment showed that "the circuit switched telephone system was totally inadequate for the job. Kleinrock's conviction of the need for packet switching was confirmed" (doc.txt).
- In late 1966, Roberts moved to DARPA and planned the ARPANET: "In late 1966 Roberts went to DARPA to develop the computer network concept and quickly put together his plan for the 'ARPANET', publishing it in 1967" (doc.txt). At the conference where he presented the paper, "Scantlebury told Roberts about the NPL work as well as that of Paul Baran and others at RAND" (doc.txt).
- After the ARPANET design was refined, "In August 1968, after Roberts and the DARPA funded community had refined the overall structure and specifications for the ARPANET, an RFQ was released by DARPA for the development of one of the key components, the packet switches called Interface Message Processors (IMP's)" (doc.txt).
- While BBN built the IMPs, "the network topology and economics were designed and optimized by Roberts working with Howard Frank and his team at Network Analysis Corporation" (doc.txt).
- In July 1972, Roberts advanced the ARPANET's first major application: "In July, Roberts expanded its utility by writing the first email utility program to list, selectively read, file, forward, and respond to messages" (doc.txt).

**Leonard Kleinrock**

- Kleinrock laid the theoretical foundation: "Leonard Kleinrock at MIT published the first paper on packet switching theory in July 1961 and the first book on the subject in 1964" (doc.txt).
- His team at UCLA prepared "the network measurement system" (doc.txt).
- "Due to Kleinrock's early development of packet switching theory and his focus on analysis, design and measurement, his Network Measurement Center at UCLA was selected to be the first node on the ARPANET" (doc.txt).
- The first node came online in September 1969: "All this came together in September 1969 when BBN installed the first IMP at UCLA and the first host computer was connected" (doc.txt).
- Kleinrock's laboratory sent the network's first host-to-host message: "One month later, when SRI was connected to the ARPANET, the first host-to-host message was sent from Kleinrock's laboratory to SRI" (doc.txt).

Together, the document presents Kleinrock as the source of the packet-switching theory and measurement work, and Roberts as the engineer and planner who built the first wide-area network experiment, designed the ARPANET at DARPA, and optimized its topology and economics.
